title: Before a Cyber Force, Fix Cyber Governance
gist: A career Navy submarine officer who served at U.S. Cyber Command argues the Cyber Force debate has its sequence backwards: the binding problem is governance — who owns cyberspace's budget, policy and accountability — not force generation. He notes that in this defense bill cycle the House declined a cyber service and instead wrote Section 1502 requiring a single accountable official, while the Senate rejected a cyber service by one vote and proposed a new Undersecretary of Defense for Cyber, Information, and Networks dual-hatted as CIO and Principal Cyber Advisor.

insights.claim: In June an amendment from Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand calling for the creation of a cyber service within the Department of the Army failed in the Senate Armed Services Committee by a single vote, while Rep. Pat Fallon has said a 'Cyber Force is inevitable.'
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: A one-vote margin means a US Cyber Force is a live near-term legislative possibility — a structural catalyst for cyber training, recruiting and IT modernization contracts if it passes.
insights.locator: Let’s not start picking out uniforms just yet

insights.claim: The highly anticipated June 2026 CSIS report skips the question of whether the Department of Defense needs a Cyber Force and goes straight to planning how to build one, building on an earlier Foundation for Defense of Democracies study, and neither fully addresses the dysfunction of cyber governance.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
entities: Center for Strategic and International Studies
insights.so_what: The most influential think-tank work has already conceded the premise, which means the public debate will under-weight governance risk in whatever is eventually legislated.
insights.locator: The highly anticipated June 2026 Center for Strategic

insights.claim: The central error in the Cyber Force conversation is conflating systemic force-generation problems — manning, training and equipping — with a separate governance problem of who owns the budget, sets policy, provides civilian oversight and accounts to Congress for the warfighting domain.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: The useful analytical split for anyone tracking defense cyber reform: force-generation fixes drive personnel and training spend, governance fixes drive who controls the money and therefore who buys.
insights.locator: The error at the center of the Cyber Force conversation

insights.claim: Asked what makes cyber so uniquely difficult, the answer is nothing except that no one owns it because everyone owns it — a structural ownership vacuum rather than technical complexity, since submarine communities are equally underwritten by complex technology.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: Undercuts the standard justification for cyber exceptionalism; if accepted, it means the answer is budget authority reallocation rather than a new service and its associated procurement pipeline.
insights.quote: except that no one owns it because everyone owns it.
insights.locator: So what makes cyber so special?

insights.claim: The Department of Defense has simultaneously treated cyberspace as so special it warrants its own combatant command and a seat at the warfighter's table, and as a commodity to be governed like enterprise information technology — a contradiction no Cyber Force design resolves.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: The warfighting-versus-utility contradiction is why DoD cyber budgets remain fragmented across Services and agencies, keeping procurement ad hoc rather than programmatic.
insights.locator: The Department has spent the last several decades

insights.claim: Cyber Command depends on the Services to generate its forces even though cyberspace will never be any Service's priority, and Cybercom 2.0 — the Department's own attempt to improve force generation — lacks the levers needed to compel the Services to prioritize a warfighting space that belongs to none of them.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: Without compulsion levers, DoD cyber readiness shortfalls persist regardless of reorganizations — a reason to expect recurring congressional intervention every defense bill cycle.
insights.locator: Start with what the advocates have gotten right

themes.theme: Where Congress is actually moving: governance, not a service

insights.claim: The House Armed Services Committee cyber subcommittee's mark of this year's defense bill, approved in early June, contains no cyber service but does contain Section 1502 directing the Secretary of Defense to establish clear accountability for the cybersecurity of Department of Defense information networks, including identification of one designated single accountable official.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: Section 1502 is the concrete legislative text to track: naming a single accountable official for DoD network cybersecurity would consolidate a currently scattered buying authority.
insights.quote: including identification of one official designated as the single accountable official
insights.locator: Congress, to its credit, has already begun addressing

insights.claim: The Senate's proposed solution is a new Undersecretary of Defense for Cyber, Information, and Networks, dual-hatted as the Department's Chief Information Officer and Principal Cyber Advisor, consolidating enterprise defense and operational advisory functions into one accountable official written into statute.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
entities: Undersecretary of Defense for Cyber, Information, and Networks
insights.so_what: If enacted, a single undersecretary would become the highest-leverage decision-maker for DoD cyber and IT spending — the office vendors and integrators would need to sell to.
insights.locator: The Senate’s possible solution is a new Undersecretary

insights.claim: Fusing the CIO and Principal Cyber Advisor roles matters because the Principal Cyber Advisor owns the cyber-operations budget while the CIO controls much of the cybersecurity and information technology budget and oversees the Services' cyber budgets — putting operations and IT priorities in the hands of one person who answers for the balance.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: Identifies exactly which budget lines would be consolidated — a concrete map of where DoD cyber money currently sits and who would control it after reform.
insights.locator: The Senate’s construct is the right skeleton

insights.claim: An undersecretary who only advises and coordinates without controlling funding would just be a more senior version of today's undefined lanes; genuine accountability requires directive authority over the domain's terrain and real ownership of the force-generation and systems dollars the Services primarily control.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
entities: Undersecretary of Defense for Cyber, Information, and Networks
insights.so_what: The test to apply to any enacted reform: does the new office control money? Without budget authority the reform is cosmetic and the fragmentation persists.
insights.quote: Otherwise, they will have picked the person to poke without giving them the authority to prevent failure.
insights.locator: But an undersecretary who only advises and coordinates

insights.claim: Given the opportunity to create a new cyber service this cycle the House declined to take it up and the Senate rejected it by the narrowest possible margin, with both chambers instead opting for the governance solution — and the same Senate committee directed reviews of whether Cyber Command is adequately organized for its expanding authorities and of the roles and resourcing of the Principal Cyber Advisors.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: Near-term legislative probability favors a new undersecretary and mandated studies over a standalone Cyber Force — position for governance reform, not a new-service buildout.
insights.locator: Now consider for a moment what both chambers did this cycle

insights.claim: Admiral Rickover's culture of accountability in the Nuclear Navy was enforceable not by force of personality but because the nuclear propulsion program had a single owner with genuine authority over the entire enterprise — reactor plants, training pipeline, industrial base, and the money that paid for all of it.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: The transferable principle: accountability cultures require single ownership of the money and the industrial base — a test worth applying to any proposed government technology reorganization.
insights.locator: I found myself preaching Admiral Rickover’s culture

insights.claim: The Air Force precedent that Cyber Force advocates cite actually cuts against them: before creating a new service, Congress first rebuilt the governance of the entire defense establishment through the National Security Act, creating the Secretary of Defense, the Department of the Air Force and a new structure of civilian oversight, and only then established the Air Force within it.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: The strongest historical argument that governance reform precedes service creation — implying a multi-year sequence before any Cyber Force procurement wave materializes.
insights.quote: Congress first rebuilt the governance of the entire defense establishment through the National Security Act
insights.locator: Cyber Force advocates often cite the Air Force as a precedent

insights.claim: The Nunn-Cohen reforms creating Special Operations Command assembled command, civilian oversight, authorities and resources as an integrated design in a single act, and gave the enterprise its own service-like funding line, Major Force Program 11 — budget authority that, arguably more than any four-star billet, converted responsibility from an org-chart abstraction into something a person could answer for.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: A dedicated funding line is the operative mechanism to watch for; a cyber equivalent of MFP-11 would be the single clearest signal that a real cyber acquisition budget has been created.
insights.locator: History points in the same direction as the Nunn-Cohen reforms

insights.claim: Cyber has accumulated components analogous to those given to special operations forces — but piecemeal over nearly two decades rather than by initial or deliberate design, leaving Congress to decide whether the pieces need continued refinement or complete reconstruction.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: Frames the binary choice facing Congress: incremental patching (status quo procurement) versus reconstruction (a discontinuity in how DoD cyber money is spent).
insights.locator: Cyber has accumulated components analogous

insights.claim: The most rigorous Cyber Force implementation study yet, drawing on dozens of the field's most qualified individuals, resolved command and control, force size, recruitment and retention models and training pipelines but could not resolve where a Cyber Force should be institutionally housed within the Department of Defense.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
entities: Center for Strategic and International Studies
insights.so_what: The unresolved housing question is the tell that governance is unsettled — expect any near-term legislation to punt the structural question again.
insights.locator: Cyber Force advocates’ own work points in this same direction

insights.claim: The proposed Cyber Force would organize, train and equip for cyber operations but would not absorb the Services' individual networks, meaning cyberspace's terrain would remain fragmented across Services whose first priorities lie elsewhere — so the founding complaint of cyber as everyone's responsibility and no one's priority would survive intact at the network layer where most operational friction lives.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: Even a successful Cyber Force would leave Service network defense unconsolidated, so enterprise network security spending stays distributed across the Services rather than centralizing.
insights.locator: The commission’s scoping decision points in the same direction

insights.claim: Testifying before a National Academies committee, former Cyber Command commanders Generals Timothy Haugh and Paul Nakasone warned that a new service risks a top-heavy bureaucracy and confusion over who defends the other Services' networks.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: Opposition from two former Cyber Command commanders materially lowers the odds of near-term Cyber Force passage.
insights.locator: Two of the community’s stewards saw the same gap

insights.claim: Designing a service in parallel with governance reform means designing against assumptions the governance debate may prove incorrect, because who owns the networks, who the customer is, and where the force-generation budget sits are all outputs of the governance decision rather than inputs to it.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: Predicts costly rework in any parallel-track approach — relevant to forecasting program instability and re-competes in cyber acquisition.
insights.quote: This is the naval equivalent of laying the keel for the first in the class while the naval architects are still arguing over the hull form.
insights.locator: Governance reform and service creation are not necessarily sequential

insights.claim: Sequencing governance reform before service creation would cost roughly two years relative to Cyber Force advocates' timeline, while a service commissioned before the governance fight is settled would inherit the fragmentation as a birth defect.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: A concrete two-year delay estimate for the governance-first path — the timeline to assume for any cyber-service-dependent business case.
insights.quote: A service commissioned before the governance fight is settled inherits the fragmentation as a birth defect, institutionalizing it right beside its brand-new flag and its birthday.
insights.locator: That sequence would cost perhaps two years

insights.claim: Congress repeats the same cyber diagnosis annually, with each annual defense bill directing another study, another commission and another attempt to patch a construct that no one will defend.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: A decade-plus pattern of studies rather than structural change is the base rate: default to expecting incrementalism in DoD cyber reform absent a forcing event.
insights.locator: More than a decade of readiness shortfalls

themes.theme: Culture as a function of structure

insights.claim: Routine tasking within the cyber enterprise required coordination with the very organizations being tasked — drafts circulated for comment, wording negotiated, seniors pulled in when consensus failed — reflecting that Cyber Command functions primarily as a coordinator among organizations that own different pieces of the problem with motivations that do not always align.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: First-hand evidence that Cyber Command lacks directive authority in practice, not just on paper — the operational reality behind slow decision cycles in DoD cyber.
insights.locator: Not long after I arrived at Cyber Command

insights.claim: Accountability culture cannot be conjured by leadership will; structure makes culture enforceable, which is why cyber's lack of a single owner over budget, terrain and training leaves accountability perpetually undefined and resourcing done on an ad hoc basis by Services, combatant commands and various agencies.
insights.speaker: Justin Hardy
insights.so_what: Explains why cyber readiness fixes that rely on leadership emphasis rather than budget authority have repeatedly failed — a filter for evaluating reform proposals.
insights.locator: Through accretion rather than design
